questions.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis in the direction of increasing $x$ where $x\ge 0.$ When the displacement of $P$ from the origin is $x\,m,$ the velocity is $v\,m/s,$ and the acceleration is $k(1-x)\,{m/s}^{2},$ where $k$ is a positive constant. If $P$ has velocity $v=\sqrt{6}\,m/s$ at the origin and has velocity $v=3\,m/s$ when its displacement is $\frac{3}{2}\,m,$ find the maximum velocity of the particle.
questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14218054/assets/75ef4755be2965b674fc7a5440ff05bb3f37d70507941eb48eeae554fcb2d538.png)

The extrema of the velocity occur at the critical points of $v.$ Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $k(1-x)\,{m/s}^{2},$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=k(1-x).
$$

To find the moments where $v$ is a maximum, we need to solve $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=0$ and test each solution using the first derivative test.

Solving $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=0$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}k(1-x) & =0 \\ 1-x & =0 \\ x & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the extremum of the velocity function occurs when $x=1\,m.$

We now test the extreme value using the first derivative test. We summarize the necessary information in a table, shown below.

| $x$ | $(0,1)$ | $1$ | $(1,\infty )$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Test Point | $\frac{1}{2}$ |  | $\frac{3}{2}$ |
| $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}$ | $\frac{k}{2}>0$ | $0$ | $-\frac{k}{2}<0$ |
| $v$ | $↗$ | max | $↘$ |

We conclude that the velocity is maximized when $x=1\,m.$

Next, using the fact that

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our initial equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=k(1-x).
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x=\int k(1-x)\,\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=k(x-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2})+C.
$$

Now, since $v=\sqrt{6}\,{m/s}^{2}$ when $x=0\,m,$ we can find the value of the constant $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =k(\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}-x)+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(\sqrt{6})^{2} & =k(0-\frac{1}{2}(0)^{2})+C \\ C & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=k(x-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2})+3.
$$

Also, since $v=3\,{m/s}^{2}$ when $x=\frac{3}{2}\,m,$ we can find the value of the positive constant $k,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =k(x-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2})+3 \\ \frac{1}{2}(3)^{2} & =k(\frac{3}{2}-\frac{1}{2}{(\frac{3}{2})}^{2})+3 \\ \frac{9}{2} & =\frac{3}{8}k+3 \\ \frac{3}{8}k & =\frac{3}{2} \\ k & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =4x-2{x}^{2}+3 \\ {v}^{2} & =8x-4{x}^{2}+6 \\ v & =\pm \sqrt{8x-4{x}^{2}+6}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the particle is moving in the direction of increasing $x,$ we have that $v(x)>0,$ so we can disregard the negative square root. Therefore,

$$
v(x)=\sqrt{8x-4{x}^{2}+6}.
$$

Finally, we calculate the maximum velocity:

$$
{v}_{max}=v(1)=\sqrt{8(1)-4(1)^{2}+6}=\sqrt{10}\,m/s.
$$

questions.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis. When the displacement of $P$ from the origin is $x\,m,$ the velocity is $v\,m/s,$ the magnitude of the acceleration is $kx\,{m/s}^{2},$ where $k$ is a positive constant, and the acceleration is directed toward $O.$ If $P$ has velocity $v=6\,m/s$ at the origin and the particle is at rest when its displacement is $3\sqrt{2}\,m,$ find the value of $k.$
questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14218054/assets/cd42eb74e5bba02951118c349a1b25f7193c39aa53f6504403918dfa984eb2c2.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ has magnitude $kx\,{m/s}^{2}$ and is directed *toward* $O,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=-kx.
$$

Using the fact that

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=-kx.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x=\int (-kx)\,\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=-\frac{k}{2}{x}^{2}+C.
$$

Now, since $v=6\,m/s$ when $x=0\,m,$ we can find the value of the constant $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =-\frac{k}{2}{x}^{2}+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(6)^{2} & =-\frac{k}{2}(0)^{3}+C \\ C & =18\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=18-\frac{k}{2}{x}^{2}.
$$

Finally, since $v=0\,m/s$ when $x=3\sqrt{2}\,m,$ we can find the value of the positive constant $k,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =18-\frac{k}{2}{x}^{2} \\ \frac{1}{2}(0)^{2} & =18-\frac{k}{2}(3\sqrt{2})^{2} \\ 18-9k & =0 \\ 9k & =18 \\ k & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis in the direction of increasing $x$ where $x\ge 0.$ When the displacement of $P$ from the origin is $x\,m,$ the velocity is $v\,m/s,$ and the acceleration is $(6-3x)\,{m/s}^{2}.$ If $P$ has velocity $v=\sqrt{2}\,m/s$ at the origin, find the maximum velocity of the particle.
questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14218054/assets/dd8eecba814fda9c628dc4c8a3853805a31e57f953dd9bf26a6fa79f5c700788.png)

The extrema of the velocity occur at the critical points of $v.$ Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $(6-3x)\,{m/s}^{2},$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=6-3x.
$$

To find the moments where $v$ is a maximum, we need to solve $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=0$ and test each solution using the first or second derivative test.

Solving $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=0$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}6-3x & =0 \\ x & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the extremum of the velocity function occurs when $x=2\,m.$

We now test the extreme value using the first derivative test. We summarize the necessary information in a table, shown below.

| $x$ | $(0,2)$ | $2$ | $(2,\infty )$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Test Point | $1$ |  | $3$ |
| $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}$ | $3>0$ | $0$ | $-3<0$ |
| $v$ | $↗$ | max | $↘$ |

We conclude that the velocity is maximized when $x=2\,m.$

Next, using the fact that

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our initial equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=6-3x.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x=\int (6-3x)\,\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=6x-\frac{3}{2}{x}^{2}+C.
$$

Now, since $v=\sqrt{2}\,m/s$ when $x=0\,m,$ we can find the value of the constant $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =6x-\frac{3}{2}{x}^{2}+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(\sqrt{2})^{2} & =6(0)-\frac{3}{2}(0)^{2}+C \\ C & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =6x-\frac{3}{2}{x}^{2}+1 \\ {v}^{2} & =12x-3{x}^{2}+2 \\ v & =\pm \sqrt{-3{x}^{2}+12x+2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the particle is moving in the direction of increasing $x,$ we have that $v(x)>0,$ so we can disregard the negative square root. Therefore,

$$
v(x)=\sqrt{-3{x}^{2}+12x+2}.
$$

Finally, we calculate the maximum velocity:

$$
{v}_{max}=v(2)=\sqrt{-3(2)^{2}+12(2)+2}=\sqrt{14}\,m/s
$$

questions.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the positive $x$-axis. When the displacement of $P$ from the origin is $x\,m,$ the velocity is $v\,m/s,$ and the acceleration is $k\sqrt{x}\,{m/s}^{2},$ where $k$ is a positive constant. If $P$ has velocity $v=6\,m/s$ at the origin and the particle has velocity $v=6\sqrt{6}\,m/s$ when its displacement is $9\,m,$ find the value of $k.$
questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14218054/assets/b052a65fb0dbcc14a5d359b693beafdf5da3f4bbe1e10f006c315e8168340d5c.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $k\sqrt{x}\,{m/s}^{2},$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=k\sqrt{x}.
$$

Using the fact that

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=k\sqrt{x}.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x=\int (k\sqrt{x})\,\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=\frac{2k}{3}{x}^{3/2}+C.
$$

Now, since $v=6\,m/s$ when $x=0\,m,$ we can find the value of the constant $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =\frac{2k}{3}{x}^{3/2}+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(6)^{2} & =\frac{2k}{3}(0)^{3/2}+C \\ C & =18\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=\frac{2k}{3}{x}^{3/2}+18.
$$

Finally, since $v=6\sqrt{6}\,m/s$ when $x=9\,m,$ we can find the value of the positive constant $k,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =\frac{2k}{3}{x}^{3/2}+18 \\ \frac{1}{2}(6\sqrt{6})^{2} & =\frac{2k}{3}(9)^{3/2}+18 \\ 108 & =18k+18 \\ 18k & =90 \\ k & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
A particle $P$ moves along the positive $x$-axis. When the displacement of $P$ from the origin is $x$ meters, its velocity is $v\,m/s,$ the magnitude of its acceleration is $6{x}^{2}\,{m/s}^{2},$ and the acceleration is directed toward $O.$
If $P$ has velocity $2\sqrt{7}\,m/s$ when its displacement is $1\,m,$ find the values of $x$ for which $P$ is instantaneously at rest.
questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14218054/assets/a8c9778580276589ff7a047ca3c7b620de842efd7b3799a70b6e4484bc5fa0e6.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ has magnitude $6{x}^{2}\,{m/s}^{2}$ and is directed *toward* $O,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=-6{x}^{2}.
$$

Using the fact that

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=-6{x}^{2}.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x=\int (-6{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=-2{x}^{3}+C.
$$

Now, since $v=2\sqrt{7}\,m/s$ when $x=1\,m,$ we can find the value of the constant $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =-2{x}^{3}+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(2\sqrt{7})^{2} & =-2(1)^{3}+C \\ C & =14+2 \\ C & =16\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=16-2{x}^{3}.
$$

Finally, the particle is instantaneously at rest when $v(x)=0\,m/s.$ We find the displacement of the particle when instantaneously at rest by substituting $v=0$ in the equation above and solving for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =16-2{x}^{3} \\ \frac{1}{2}(0)^{2} & =16-2{x}^{3} \\ 2{x}^{3} & =16 \\ {x}^{3} & =8 \\ x & =2\,m.\end{aligned}
$$
